title: Traditional Kenyan Suqaar
community: Somali-Kenyan — widely enjoyed in Nairobi and North Eastern Kenya
author: Chef Fadumo Hassan

regionalMap.primaryRegion: North Eastern Kenya — Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Isiolo
regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Nairobi's Eastleigh neighbourhood and in Somali-Kenyan communities nationwide

heritage.history: Suqaar is a cornerstone of Somali cuisine that has become deeply woven into the food culture of North Eastern Kenya. The dish reflects the nomadic pastoral traditions of the Somali people, who have herded camels, goats, and cattle across the Horn of Africa for centuries. Quick to prepare, rich in protein, and deeply satisfying, Suqaar was the ideal food for communities on the move. In Kenya, it is most associated with Eastleigh in Nairobi and the North Eastern counties, where Somali-Kenyan communities have built a vibrant food culture.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally prepared with goat or camel meat, modern Suqaar in Kenyan restaurants uses beef, chicken, or lamb and is widely available in Nairobi's Somali restaurants. It has gained popularity across communities for its quick preparation and rich flavour.

desc: Suqaar is one of Northern Kenya's most beloved dishes — tender cubes of beef or goat quickly stir-fried with onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and a warming blend of cumin, cardamom, and coriander until perfectly cooked and fragrant. Fast, rich, and deeply satisfying.
longDesc: Suqaar is the dish that teaches you how much flavour can be achieved in under 30 minutes. Unlike the slow braises of other Kenyan meat dishes, Suqaar is a quick, high-heat stir-fry — tender cubes of meat cooked fast in a spiced tomato base until just done. The result is remarkably juicy and fragrant. In Eastleigh, Nairobi's vibrant Somali neighbourhood, the smell of Suqaar frying in the evening is as defining as any in the city.
ingredients: 600g beef sirloin, rump, or goat — cut into 1–2 cm cubes
1 green or red bell pepper — diced

substitutions.alternative: Goat, lamb, or boneless chicken thighs
Green chilli for a spicier version
Omit or use a tiny pinch of ground cinnamon

steps: Pat the meat cubes completely dry with paper towels. Season with salt, black pepper, cumin, coriander, cardamom, paprika, and turmeric. Toss to coat evenly.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan or skillet over high heat until shimmering.
Add the seasoned meat cubes in a single layer. Do not stir immediately — allow to sear for 2 minutes until browned on the bottom.
Toss and cook for another 2–3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until browned on all sides. The meat should be just cooked through — do not overcook. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan over medium heat, add the onions. Cook for 4–5 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced tomatoes and bell pepper. Cook for 4–6 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a light sauce.
Return the cooked meat to the pan. Toss everything together and cook for 2–3 minutes, allowing the flavours to come together.
Squeeze in the lemon juice. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Scatter with fresh coriander and serve immediately with rice, canjeero, or chapati.
chefTips: High heat and a hot pan are essential — Suqaar is a stir-fry, not a stew. The meat should sear, not steam.
Cut the meat into small, uniform cubes so they cook evenly in the short cooking time.
Do not overcook the meat — the moment it is just cooked through, remove it from the pan. Overcooked Suqaar becomes tough and dry.
Season the raw meat first and let the spices coat it before it hits the hot pan.
commonMistakes: Overcrowding the pan — lowers the temperature, causing the meat to steam and become tough.
Cooking on low heat — Suqaar must be cooked on high heat for the right texture and caramelisation.
Overcooking the meat — small cubes cook very quickly and should be removed the moment they are done.
Adding meat and vegetables to the pan at the same time — they cook at different rates and the result is uneven.

faqs.a: Suqaar is a Somali word referring to meat cut into small cubes and quickly cooked. It is one of the most widely eaten dishes in Somali cuisine and a staple of Somali-Kenyan communities.
Yes — camel is the traditional meat in northern Somali communities. It has a distinctive flavour and a slightly firmer texture. Treat it exactly like beef in this recipe.

Canjeero (also called anjero or lahoh) is a traditional Somali fermented flatbread, similar to Ethiopian injera but lighter. It is the most traditional accompaniment to Suqaar and is used to scoop the meat and sauce.

faqs.q: How is Suqaar different from Nyama Choma?
faqs.a: Nyama Choma is whole pieces of meat grilled slowly over charcoal. Suqaar is small cubes of meat quickly stir-fried in a pan with spices and vegetables. They are completely different cooking methods and flavour profiles.

cookingScience: Suqaar uses high-heat stir-frying to achieve the Maillard reaction — the browning of proteins and sugars on the meat surface that creates hundreds of new flavour compounds. This is why high heat and a dry, uncrowded pan are essential. Water on the meat surface or a crowded pan drops the temperature and causes steaming instead of searing, producing grey, flavourless meat rather than the browned, caramelised result that defines great Suqaar.
sustainabilityTips: Suqaar works beautifully with less premium cuts of beef — reducing food waste by making the most of tougher, cheaper cuts through high-heat cooking.
Buy meat from local halal butchers who source from Kenyan farmers when possible.
Leftover Suqaar makes an outstanding filling for chapati wraps or rice bowls the next day.
storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 2 months.
reheating: Reheat quickly in a hot pan with a splash of oil for 2–3 minutes. Avoid microwave if possible — it makes the meat tough.
healthBenefits: High in complete protein — 32g per serving from beef or goat.
Rich in iron, zinc, and vitamin B12 — essential for energy, immunity, and nerve health.
Bell peppers and tomatoes provide vitamin C and antioxidants.
Cumin and coriander add digestive and anti-inflammatory benefits.
Naturally low in carbohydrates — 3g per serving.
culturalNote: Suqaar is a defining dish of Somali-Kenyan food culture and is closely associated with North Eastern Kenya and Nairobi's Eastleigh neighbourhood. It reflects the pastoral traditions of the Somali people — a cuisine built on meat, spice, and the practical needs of communities who have moved across vast landscapes for centuries. In Kenya, Suqaar represents the rich cultural contribution of the Somali-Kenyan community to the country's diverse food heritage.
regionalVariations: Classic beef Suqaar — the most common version in Kenya.
Goat Suqaar — the traditional pastoral version.
Camel Suqaar — the most traditional northern Somali version.
Chicken Suqaar — lighter and quicker, popular in urban restaurants.
Suqaar with potatoes — cubed potatoes added for a heartier meal.
Spicy Suqaar — with extra chilli and pepper for heat lovers.
